attributes.what: TRUE or FALSE: is a SAML 1.1 sign-in this relying party started — the Shibboleth 1.3 AuthnRequest profile, a request carrying shire — answered, overriding saml11.spInitiatedSso. The request is an unsigned URL, so FALSE closes the door rather than proving who opened it.

attributes.name: samlAuthnRequestSigned
attributes.what: TRUE when the last AuthnRequest from this service provider carried a signature — an enveloped ds:Signature on the POST binding, or the Signature parameter of section 3.4.4.1 on the Redirect binding. ASSIGNED rather than accumulated, because it is a fact about the last request and a history of booleans would say nothing.

attributes.name: wsfedRealm
attributes.what: THE WTREALM from a wsignin1.0 request (section 13.2.1) — WS-Federation's identifier attribute. Accumulates, for the reason every identifier here does.

attributes.name: wsfedReplyUrl
attributes.from: WS-Federation, the console, or by hand
attributes.what: WHERE A SIGN-IN RESPONSE IS POSTED BACK TO for this application: the `wreply` of section 13.2.1, WS-Federation's redirect URI. It was written into samlAssertionConsumerService until 2026-08-25, which put a wreply in the attribute the SAML pages read for an assertion consumer service and for the Single Logout fallback — one attribute holding two protocols' return addresses, so a WS-Federation application appeared to have a SAML ACS it had never named. Two facts, two attributes. Like the SAML one beside it this is CHECKED IN PRODUCT MODE ONLY: development refuses no wreply, because a service that refused would remove a test case rather than add one; product posts only to an address on this list and a sighting never adds one. A wreply development recorded is marked on appReturnAddressObserved and product refuses it until it is confirmed; values recorded before that mark existed carry none and still need reviewing before a realm is switched to product.

attributes.name: wsfedIdpInitiatedSso
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.what: TRUE or FALSE: may this identity provider START a sign-in to this relying party — /wsfed/initiate/{rp} or /launch/{app}, posting to its registered wsfedReplyUrl — overriding wsfed.idpInitiatedSso.

attributes.name: wsfedSpInitiatedSso
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.what: TRUE or FALSE: is this relying party's own wsignin1.0 answered, overriding wsfed.spInitiatedSso. A wsignin1.0 is an unsigned URL, so FALSE closes the door rather than proving who opened it.

attributes.name: wsfedSsoConsent
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.what: TRUE or FALSE: is a person asked, once, before WS-Federation signs them in to this application from a session they already have, overriding wsfed.ssoConsent (ASVS 5.0.0 7.6.2). FALSE suits an application everybody in the realm is expected to use; a global consent on the entry answers for everyone and keeps the record of who agreed.

attributes.name: wsfedSignOutUri
attributes.what:
WHERE A wsignoutcleanup1.0 PING IS SENT for this application — WS-Federation's logout URI, and the one this table did not have until 2026-08-30. DECLARED, not observed, which makes it the sibling of samlSingleLogoutService rather than of wsfedReplyUrl: a cleanup is sent when a SESSION ends, and by then the request that would have carried a wreply is long over.

**A DECLARED ADDRESS OUTRANKS AN OBSERVED ONE** (#747). `cleanupTargetsFor()` pings every value here for a realm the session signed into, and the wreply the sign-in response went to, which `session.wsfedRealms` records, only where this is empty.

attributes.name: wstrustAppliesTo
attributes.what:
THE APPLIESTO ADDRESS from a RequestSecurityToken — the service the token is issued FOR, and WS-Trust's identifier attribute. Accumulates.

**IT IS READ**, which it was not before 2026-08-27, and it is `oauthAudience`'s exception arriving through a second protocol: an OnBehalfOf or ActAs asking for a token to reach `https://esb.example.com` is recorded on /admin/delegation against the APPLICATION that registered that address, so a chain of delegated hops draws as one picture rather than as boxes named after URLs that nothing else in it mentions. In development a LOOKUP and not a permission — an AppliesTo nobody registered is issued for and recorded verbatim; in product it is refused (#496). See forAppliesTo(), which asks this attribute first and `samlEntityId` behind it.

attributes.name: wstrustJwtScope
attributes.what:
THE OAUTH 2.0 SCOPES A WS-TRUST JWT FOR THIS APPLICATION CARRIES, one scope value each (#485). A JWT WS-Trust issues with this application as the AppliesTo (wst:TokenType urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:jwt) carries them in its `scope` claim, space-delimited (RFC 9068 section 2.2.3); with none set it carries no `scope`. A SAML token is unaffected.

**EACH IS JUDGED AS AN OAUTH ACCESS TOKEN'S IS**, with this application as the client: `oauthAllowedScope` declares what it may be issued (in product; this service's protected scopes in every mode), and the issuance policy's per-scope question decides. A value the policy drops is LEFT OFF the token and audited (STS-OAUTH-0579), never issued. A write naming an undeclared scope is accepted here, because the declaration may change and development grants undeclared scopes: declare it on oauthAllowedScope too. A value the policy will drop is WARNED about where it is set (#488): beside this field, in the Save reply, and as `warnings` on the /admin-api write replies and the application's view.

attributes.name: krb5ServicePrincipalName
attributes.what: THE SPN, e.g. HTTP/sts@EXAMPLE.COM — Kerberos v5's identifier attribute. A Kerberos service is an application like the others here, and it is the one whose identifier this service may have created on demand (KRB5_SERVICE_DOMAINS). It accumulates, and here that is the ordinary case rather than the unusual one: one service commonly answers to several SPNs — HTTP/host and HTTP/host.example.com — and a real KDC holds them all against one account.

attributes.name: krb5ClaimsPac
attributes.from: the console's Kerberos PAC claims section
attributes.what: THIS SERVICE'S OWN PAC CLAIMS, as a JSON array of rows like the realm's Kerberos PAC claims page. Added to the claims a service ticket for one of this application's SPNs carries (those of the TGT it was issued from), an application row replacing the claim of the same name. Only while krb5.pacClaims is on.

attributes.name: gnapClaimsAccessToken
attributes.what: THIS CLIENT'S OWN GNAP ACCESS-TOKEN JWT CLAIMS, as a JSON array of rows like the other custom-claim sets. Added to a jwt-signed token and to the JWT inside a jwt-encrypted token issued to this client, an application row replacing the realm row of the same name. The token's own claims (access, flags, label, grant_id and the JWT names) cannot be overridden. Macaroon, biscuit and zcap tokens do not carry these rows.

attributes.name: krb5TrustedForDelegation
attributes.what: TRUE or FALSE, default FALSE: this Kerberos service is TRUSTED FOR DELEGATION — unconstrained (Active Directory's TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION). Its service tickets carry ok-as-delegate, which tells a client it may forward its TGT here; whoever holds a forwarded TGT can act as that person anywhere. A protected person's TGT is never forwardable, so it is never forwarded however this is set. Constrained delegation (appAllowedToDelegateTo, appAllowedToActOnBehalfOf) is the safer alternative.

attributes.name: krb5S4uSelfRealm
attributes.familyWhy: S4U2Self is a Kerberos request ([MS-SFU]).
attributes.what: THE KERBEROS REALMS WHOSE USERS THIS SERVICE MAY OBTAIN S4U2SELF TICKETS FOR, beside its own. EMPTY MEANS ITS OWN REALM ONLY. A value must be a realm this realm's trusts accept tickets from — a trust holding an incoming key, or a realm a transitive one routes — and is checked at the write.

attributes.name: krb5ForeignTgtDelegation
attributes.familyWhy: ok-as-delegate and forwarded TGTs are Kerberos's.
attributes.what: `inherit` (the default) or `deny`: what this service says of a TGT delegated to it ACROSS A TRUST — ok-as-delegate on its tickets for a user of another realm. `inherit` follows the trust's attributes ([MS-KILE] 3.3.5.7.5); `deny` refuses it whatever they say. It only narrows: nothing here enables what the trust does not.

attributes.name: krb5ServiceKeys
attributes.what: A SERVICE PRINCIPAL'S RANDOM LONG-TERM KEYS, one per enctype, in ONE value: a JSON document naming the SPN, the realm and the kvno beside the keys, SEALED under the key-encryption key wherever that key outlives the process. One value rather than one per enctype so that a key cannot be moved onto another entry or another kvno without the seal failing. Password-equivalent: it is WITHHELD from every page and every /admin-api reply, and the one time it leaves this service is as the keytab a create or a rotate hands over.

attributes.name: krb5ServiceKeyInfo
attributes.what: What `krb5ServiceKeys` holds, without the keys: the kvno, the enctypes, when the keys were made and whether they are sealed. Written in the same act as the keys, so the two cannot describe different generations.

attributes.name: appEnrolledCertificate
attributes.what: One JSON record per certificate issued to this application over an enrollment protocol: serial, protocol, profile, subject, names, validity, who asked, whether the key was generated here, the certificate and its issuing chain, and a revocation mark. Public material. Written by common/cert_enrollment.ts only.

attributes.name: appEnrolledPrivateKey
attributes.what: A private key THIS SERVICE generated for one of the certificates above (EST server-side key generation, or the console's server-generated key pair), as `<serial>:<PEM>`, sealed wherever the key-encryption key outlives the process. WITHHELD from every page and /admin-api reply; it is handed over once, at issuance.

attributes.name: appAcmeEabKey
attributes.what: ACME External Account Binding keys issued for this application, one JSON record each: the key id, the sealed HMAC key, its expiry and the account it bound. A working credential, WITHHELD from every page and /admin-api reply.

attributes.name: appScepChallenge
attributes.what: SCEP challenge passwords issued for this application, one JSON record each: the id, a SHA-256 digest of the secret, the profile, the expiry and when it was redeemed. WITHHELD from every page and /admin-api reply.

attributes.name: appCertificateHostName
attributes.what: A DNS name or IP address this application may be issued a certificate for over ACME, EST or SCEP. Registering one is the whole proof of control: this service never dials a name to validate it. Set by an administrator; read by common/cert_enrollment.ts.

attributes.name: appRegistrationJson
attributes.what: THE RFC 7591 REGISTRATION VERBATIM, as JSON on one attribute. It is here because RFC 7591 lets a client register arbitrary metadata and RFC 7592's read has to hand back what was registered — which no fixed set of LDAP attributes can represent. It is the STARTING POINT when the record is reconstructed and not the last word: every member that also has an attribute above is then overwritten FROM that attribute, so an ldapmodify of oauthRedirectUri is what RFC 9700 mode enforces. Edit this only to change a member that has no attribute of its own.

attributes.name: appRegistrationAccessToken
attributes.what: The RFC 7592 registration access token, which is what guards the read, update and delete operations on this client. Sealed like oauthClientSecret wherever the process holds a durable key-encryption key (since 2026-10-01), and never written to the audit log.

attributes.name: oid4vpClientId
attributes.what: THE VERIFIER'S CLIENT_ID in an Authorization Request asking for a presentation — OpenID4VP's identifier attribute. This service's own Verifier takes its from configuration (oid4vp.clientId) rather than from a caller, so that record appears the first time a presentation is verified; a value declared here is a FOREIGN verifier somebody is configuring.

attributes.name: federationPartnerId
attributes.what: WHAT A FEDERATION PARTNER CALLS ITSELF — a foreign identity provider's entityID, or its issuer identifier where the relationship speaks OpenID Connect. THE RELATIONSHIP IS NOT HERE: the endpoints, the certificate and the attribute mapping live under ou=federations and are what /federation/acs/{id} actually verifies against (see federation/CLAUDE.md). This entry is the partner as a PARTY, and this attribute is the name it goes by — so a value here federates with nobody, which is the one place in this service where that sentence has teeth.

attributes.name: ldapBindDn
attributes.what: THE DN A DIRECTORY CLIENT BINDS AS on 389 or LDAPS 636. Nothing will ever write this and nothing will ever read it: in development mode EVERY BIND SUCCEEDS — any DN, any password, anonymous — and in product mode only a person binds, so an application reads the directory through SCIM instead. It is where an operator records which credential an application is expected to use, beside the rest of what that application is.

attributes.name: scimClientId
attributes.what: WHAT A PROVISIONING CLIENT AT /scim/v2 IS CALLED — the OAuth client_id it presents a token from, or the username it sends in Basic. That surface authenticates its CALLER in any of the six schemes RFC 7644 section 2 names rather than an application identifier, so it writes nothing here; the value is a declaration, and the SCIM gate is what decides whether a credential is demanded at all.

attributes.name: acmeAllowedProfiles
attributes.what: THE ACME PROFILES THIS APPLICATION MAY BE ISSUED. Where it lists something it OVERRIDES acme.allowedProfiles for this application, wider or narrower; empty leaves the realm's list. The five CA, OCSP and KDC profiles are never issued.

attributes.name: acmeDefaultProfile
attributes.what: THE PROFILE THIS APPLICATION IS ISSUED OVER ACME WHEN A REQUEST NAMES NONE, overriding acme.defaultProfile. Used only while the list in force for it allows it.

attributes.name: acmeCertificateLifetimeDays
attributes.what: How long a certificate this application is issued over ACME is valid, in days, overriding acme.certificateLifetimeDays (longer or shorter). No certificate outlives its Issuing CA.

attributes.name: estAllowedProfiles
attributes.what: THE EST PROFILES THIS APPLICATION MAY BE ISSUED. Where it lists something it OVERRIDES est.allowedProfiles for this application, wider or narrower; empty leaves the realm's list. The five CA, OCSP and KDC profiles are never issued.

attributes.name: estDefaultProfile
attributes.what: THE PROFILE THIS APPLICATION IS ISSUED OVER EST WHEN A REQUEST NAMES NONE, overriding est.defaultProfile. Used only while the list in force for it allows it.

attributes.name: estCertificateLifetimeDays
attributes.what: How long a certificate this application is issued over EST is valid, in days, overriding est.certificateLifetimeDays (longer or shorter). No certificate outlives its Issuing CA.

attributes.name: scepAllowedProfiles
attributes.what: THE SCEP PROFILES THIS APPLICATION MAY BE ISSUED. Where it lists something it OVERRIDES scep.allowedProfiles for this application, wider or narrower; empty leaves the realm's list. The five CA, OCSP and KDC profiles are never issued.

attributes.name: scepDefaultProfile
attributes.what: THE PROFILE THIS APPLICATION IS ISSUED OVER SCEP WHEN A REQUEST NAMES NONE, overriding scep.defaultProfile. Used only while the list in force for it allows it.

attributes.name: scepCertificateLifetimeDays
attributes.what: How long a certificate this application is issued over SCEP is valid, in days, overriding scep.certificateLifetimeDays (longer or shorter). No certificate outlives its Issuing CA.

attributes.name: estBasicAuthentication
attributes.what: Whether EST accepts this application's client id and secret (HTTP Basic, RFC 7030 section 3.2.3), overriding est.basicAuthentication: TRUE accepts it and FALSE refuses it whatever the realm says; unset leaves the realm to decide.

attributes.name: estCertificateAuthentication
attributes.what: Whether EST accepts a certificate this realm issued this application (TLS client authentication, RFC 7030 section 3.3.2), overriding est.certificateAuthentication: TRUE accepts it and FALSE refuses it; unset leaves the realm to decide.

attributes.name: estServerKeyGeneration
attributes.what: Whether EST /serverkeygen (RFC 7030 section 4.4) may generate this application's key, overriding est.serverKeyGeneration: TRUE allows it and FALSE refuses it; unset leaves the realm to decide.

attributes.name: enrollMaxCertificates
attributes.what: How many unexpired enrolled certificates (ACME, EST and SCEP together) this application may hold, overriding pki.enrollmentMaxCertificatesPerEntry (higher or lower).

attributes.name: didPublicKeyJwk
attributes.from: the console's Generate a key pair, or by hand
attributes.what: A PUBLIC KEY THE APPLICATION'S DID DOCUMENT PUBLISHES, one JWK per value, each a JsonWebKey2020 verification method named by its kid (its RFC 7638 thumbprint where it carries none) and listed under authentication and assertionMethod. Public members only: a value carrying d, p, q, dp, dq, qi, oth, k or priv is refused. Generate a key pair on the application's page and the private half is handed out once and not kept here.

attributes.name: didPrivateKeys
attributes.from: the console's Generate a key pair
attributes.what: THE PRIVATE HALVES OF THE DID KEYS THIS SERVICE GENERATED, as a JSON array of private JWKs, SEALED at rest under the key-encryption key like an application's RFC 7523 key pair. Kept so this service can sign the application's Domain Linkage Credentials (the DIF Well-Known DID Configuration) on request; a key pasted into didPublicKeyJwk by hand has no private half here and cannot sign one. Written by Generate a key pair only.

attributes.name: didService
attributes.what: A SERVICE THE DID DOCUMENT NAMES, as <type>|<serviceEndpoint>: for example LinkedDomains|https://app.example.com. The type is one token; the endpoint an absolute http or https URL. Each becomes a service entry with the id <did>#service-<n>.

attributes.name: didAlsoKnownAs
attributes.what: ANOTHER IDENTIFIER FOR THE SAME APPLICATION, published as the DID document's alsoKnownAs: an absolute URI such as the application's web origin or its client_id URL. DID Core makes it a claim, not a proof; a relying party checks it.

attributes.name: secretDestProvider
attributes.from: Directory → Secret destinations, the console, or by hand
attributes.what: WHICH SECRETS MANAGER THIS DESTINATION IS: aws (Secrets Manager, PutSecretValue), gcp (Secret Manager, AddSecretVersion), azure (Key Vault, setSecret), vault (a HashiCorp Vault or OpenBao KV version 2 engine, a write with check-and-set) or file (development mode only). A key management service is not a destination: it stores keys, not secrets.

attributes.name: secretDestPayload
attributes.from: Directory → Secret destinations, the console, or by hand
attributes.what: WHAT A PUSH WRITES: password (the bare password, the default) or json — {"username", "password", "realm", "rotatedAt"}, the object a reader takes the password out of by its field, as this service's own secret reads do (keys.kekField and the like). In Vault, whose versions are maps, password writes the one field secretDestField names.

attributes.name: secretDestRegion
attributes.from: Directory → Secret destinations, the console, or by hand
attributes.what: aws: the AWS region the secrets are in (us-east-1).

attributes.name: secretDestProject
attributes.from: Directory → Secret destinations, the console, or by hand
attributes.what: gcp: the project a short secret name is in, so that a service account names its secret as sts-svc-backup rather than projects/<project>/secrets/sts-svc-backup. A full resource name is taken as it is.

attributes.name: secretDestEndpoint
attributes.from: Directory → Secret destinations, the console, or by hand
attributes.what: azure: the vault URL (https://<name>.vault.azure.net). vault: the Vault or OpenBao address (https://vault.example.com:8200). https only — the write credential and a password cross it.

attributes.name: secretDestMount
attributes.from: Directory → Secret destinations, the console, or by hand
attributes.what: vault: where the KV version 2 engine is mounted; secret when empty.

attributes.name: secretDestField
attributes.from: Directory → Secret destinations, the console, or by hand
attributes.what: vault, with the password payload: the field of the version the password is written to; value when empty, which is the field this service's own Vault reads default to.

attributes.name: secretDestDirectory
attributes.from: Directory → Secret destinations, the console, or by hand
attributes.what: file (DEVELOPMENT MODE ONLY): the absolute directory a secret name is a file in. The file must already exist; a name that leaves the directory is refused.

attributes.name: secretDestCaCertificates
attributes.from: Directory → Secret destinations, the console, or by hand
attributes.what: vault: the PEM certificates of the CA the Vault listener chains to, trusted beside the public roots. Certificates are public; the certificate is always verified.

attributes.name: secretDestCredential
attributes.from: Directory → Secret destinations, the console, or by hand
attributes.what: THE DESTINATION'S WRITE CREDENTIAL, which may write versions of named secrets and should be able to do nothing else: aws, a JSON {"accessKeyId", "secretAccessKey"[, "sessionToken"]}; gcp, a service account key file's JSON; azure, a JSON {"tenantId", "clientId", "clientSecret"}; vault, a token. Separate from the read-only credentials this service reads its own key-encryption key and database password with. Sealed with the key-encryption key when keys persist, WITHHELD from every page, /admin-api reply and directory read, and never logged.

attributes.name: scimClientBaseUrl
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: THE REMOTE SCIM BASE URI (RFC 7644 section 1.3), the /v2 segment included where the service provider uses one: https://idp.example.com/scim/v2. https only (section 7.2); no query, fragment or user information (section 7.1).

attributes.name: scimClientEnabled
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: TRUE to push changes and reconcile; FALSE (the default) keeps the configuration and sends nothing.

attributes.name: scimClientAuthMethod
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: HOW A REQUEST IS AUTHENTICATED (RFC 7644 section 2): basic (HTTP Basic with scimClientUsername and scimClientPassword), oauth2 (a client_credentials token from scimClientTokenEndpoint, sent as a Bearer token), or none (only the TLS client certificate, when one is configured).

attributes.name: scimClientUsername
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: basic: the user name the service provider knows this client by.

attributes.name: scimClientPassword
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: basic: the password. Sealed with the key-encryption key when keys persist, WITHHELD from every page, /admin-api reply and directory read, and never logged.

attributes.name: scimClientTokenEndpoint
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: oauth2: the token endpoint of the authorization server the service provider trusts. https only.

attributes.name: scimClientOAuthClientId
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: oauth2: the client_id this client is registered under there.

attributes.name: scimClientOAuthClientSecret
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: oauth2: the client secret. Sealed, withheld and never logged.

attributes.name: scimClientOAuthClientAuth
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: oauth2: how the client authenticates at the token endpoint — client_secret_basic (the default) or client_secret_post (RFC 6749 section 2.3.1).

attributes.name: scimClientOAuthScope
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: oauth2: the scope asked for, space-separated (scim:write, for this service's own /scim/v2). Empty asks for none.

attributes.name: scimClientOAuthResource
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: oauth2: an RFC 8707 resource indicator sent with the token request, where the authorization server wants one.

attributes.name: scimClientTlsSource
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: THE TLS CLIENT CERTIFICATE presented to the service provider: none (the default), issued (by this realm's CA, from its tls-client Issuing CA, revocable on /admin/pki) or uploaded (scimClientTlsCertificate and scimClientTlsPrivateKey). It is presented whatever scimClientAuthMethod says.

attributes.name: scimClientTlsCertificate
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: The client certificate, PEM, its chain after it. Public.

attributes.name: scimClientTlsPrivateKey
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: The client certificate's private key, PEM. Sealed, withheld and never logged.

attributes.name: scimClientCaCertificates
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: PEM certificates of a CA the service provider's TLS certificate chains to, trusted beside the public roots. The certificate and its host name are always verified.

attributes.name: scimClientScopeMode
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: WHO IS PUSHED: all (every person in the realm), groups (the members of scimClientScopeGroups) or filter (the people scimClientScopeFilter matches). Somebody who leaves the scope is deprovisioned there.

attributes.name: scimClientScopeGroups
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: groups scope: the groups whose members are pushed, each a group's cn or DN.

attributes.name: scimClientScopeFilter
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: filter scope: an RFC 4515 LDAP filter a person's entry must match, such as (department=Sales).

attributes.name: scimClientGroupMode
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: WHICH GROUPS ARE PUSHED, each with its in-scope members only: none, selected (scimClientGroups), member-groups (every group an in-scope person is in) or all.

attributes.name: scimClientGroups
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: selected groups: each a group's cn or DN.

attributes.name: scimClientDeprovision
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: WHAT HAPPENS THERE when a person is deleted here or leaves the scope: deactivate (active false, the default) or delete. A disabled account here is always active false there.

attributes.name: scimClientReconcileMinutes
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: HOW OFTEN THE WHOLE SCOPE IS RECONCILED, in minutes, by the cluster scheduler: every person and group in scope is pushed, and what the service provider holds under an externalId of this realm's and no longer in scope is deprovisioned. 0 (the default) reconciles only when an administrator asks.

attributes.name: scimClientJurisdiction
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: WHERE THE SERVICE PROVIDER IS, as a jurisdiction code of the cell map (us, eu, ca, …). In a service deployed as cells, each person's home cell asks the issuance policy whether that person's data may go there (release-attributes, purpose scim-provision) before it pushes them; a refusal leaves them out of scope — not pushed, and deprovisioned if they were. Empty is an unknown jurisdiction, which the strict default never releases to. Ignored when the service is one cell.

attributes.name: scimClientCells
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: WHICH CELLS PUSH TO THE SERVICE PROVIDER, each a cell id; none (the default) means every cell. A cell not listed sends nothing for this client, so the people homed there are not pushed. Ignored when the service is one cell.

attributes.name: scimClientMaxRequestsPerSecond
attributes.from: Protocols → SCIM → Clients, or by hand
attributes.what: HOW MANY REQUESTS A SECOND the service provider is sent, at most: every delivery, lookup, discovery read and reconciliation page waits for its turn rather than failing. Empty or 0 (the default) is no limit. In a service deployed as cells each cell that pushes may send this divided by the number of such cells, rounded up.

attributes.name: ssfReceiverId
attributes.from: SSF, the console, or by hand
attributes.what: WHAT A SHARED SIGNALS RECEIVER IS CALLED — whatever it authenticated as when it created a stream at /ssf/stream, which is also the `aud` of every Security Event Token that stream carries. Unlike the four declaration-only identifiers above it, this one IS written by the protocol: creating a stream records a sighting, because a receiver authenticating and being agreed a stream is exactly the kind of event this registry exists to hold. It still grants nothing — a stream is what decides what a receiver gets, and it carries its own audience.

attributes.name: ssfDeliveryEndpoint
attributes.what: WHERE THIS RECEIVER EXPECTS ITS EVENTS PUSHED — an RFC 8935 delivery endpoint. It is a DECLARATION and nothing reads it: a push goes to the endpoint on the STREAM, which the receiver named when it created one, and this service will not take a URL to dial from an application entry: a URL recorded here is a note about what a receiver is, and a URL on a stream is a URL this service opens a connection to. The two are deliberately not the same store.

attributes.name: ssfAllowedEvents
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It limits which Security Event Tokens a stream owned by this application is sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would sit there reading like a limit that was in force.
attributes.what: WHICH SHARED SIGNALS EVENT TYPES A STREAM OWNED BY THIS APPLICATION MAY BE SENT. One value per line, each either a whole profile — `caep` (the eight session events) or `risc` (the fourteen account events) — or one event type URI, such as https://schemas.openid.net/secevent/caep/event-type/session-revoked. EMPTY MEANS UNRESTRICTED. SSF's own verification and stream-updated events are always allowed. It is ENFORCED twice: a stream this application creates or updates is agreed only the types allowed here (anything else it asked for is absent from `events_delivered`, and the stream's log says why), and every delivery checks it again, so removing a value stops existing streams receiving that type. The owner is whoever authenticated to /ssf/stream, matched against this entry's identifier or its ssfReceiverId values.

attributes.name: ssfCaepIncludeReasons
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: TRUE or FALSE: send reason_admin and reason_user on the CAEP events this receiver's streams carry. Both are OPTIONAL members (CAEP 1.0 section 2), so either answer conforms.

attributes.name: ssfCaepReasonLanguage
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: The BCP 47 language tag the CAEP reason members are keyed under on this receiver's streams. They stay objects keyed by a tag either way.

attributes.name: ssfCaepOmitEventTimestamp
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: TRUE or FALSE: leave event_timestamp (OPTIONAL, CAEP 1.0 section 2) off the CAEP events this receiver's streams carry.

attributes.name: ssfRiscIncludeReasons
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: TRUE or FALSE: send reason_admin and reason_user on the RISC events that define them, on this receiver's streams.

attributes.name: ssfRiscReasonLanguage
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: The BCP 47 language tag the RISC reason members are keyed under on this receiver's streams.

attributes.name: ssfRiscOmitEventTimestamp
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: TRUE or FALSE: leave event_timestamp off the RISC events that define it, on this receiver's streams.

attributes.name: ssfSigningAlgorithm
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: The JWS algorithm this receiver's Security Event Tokens are signed with. Each is one this transmitter publishes a key for in its JWKS, so the receiver can always verify.

attributes.name: ssfMinVerificationInterval
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: Seconds: min_verification_interval (SSF 1.0 section 8.1.1, transmitter-supplied) on this receiver's streams. A receiver asking for a shorter one is refused.

attributes.name: ssfInactivityTimeoutS
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: Seconds: inactivity_timeout (SSF 1.0 section 8.1.1, transmitter-supplied) on this receiver's streams; 0 means none.

attributes.name: ssfInactivityAction
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: What happens to one of this receiver's streams when its inactivity timeout passes.

attributes.name: ssfVerificationEveryS
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: Seconds between the verification events this transmitter sends on this receiver's streams by itself; 0 means none.

attributes.name: ssfStreamStatusOnCreate
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: The status a stream this receiver creates starts in.

attributes.name: ssfMaxStreams
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: How many streams this receiver may hold at once.

attributes.name: ssfMaxSubjectsPerStream
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: How many subjects one of this receiver's streams may name.

attributes.name: ssfMaxQueuedEvents
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: How many undelivered events one of this receiver's streams holds.

attributes.name: ssfPollMaxEvents
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: The most events one poll of this receiver's stream returns (RFC 8936 lets a transmitter return fewer than maxEvents).

attributes.name: ssfDeadLetterMaxPerStream
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: How many dead letters one of this receiver's streams keeps.

attributes.name: ssfPushTimeoutMs
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: Milliseconds to wait for this receiver's push endpoint to answer.

attributes.name: ssfPushRetries
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: How many times a failed push to this receiver is tried again before it becomes a dead letter.

attributes.name: ssfPushRetryDelayMs
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.familyWhy: It changes what this application's Shared Signals streams are sent, so on an entry declared for no Shared Signals family it would read like a setting in force.
attributes.what: Milliseconds between push attempts to this receiver.

attributes.name: gnapInstanceId
attributes.what: A STATIC instance identifier (RFC 9635 section 2.3.1): the string a client sends as `client` in place of its key. The key it must then prove is gnapKey or gnapKeyReference on this entry. Dynamic identifiers the authorization server hands out (section 3.5) are not written here.

attributes.name: gnapKey
attributes.from: GNAP (on first sight, development), the console, or by hand
attributes.what: The client instance's or resource server's PUBLIC key, as the JSON key object of RFC 9635 section 7.1: a proof method and exactly one of jwk, cert or cert#S256. It is how a request by value is matched to this entry, by the key's thumbprint.

attributes.name: gnapKeyIdentity
attributes.what: The thumbprint identity of gnapKey (jkt:... for a JWK, x5t:... for a certificate), written when GNAP creates the entry so the key can be found without re-reading it.

attributes.name: gnapKeyReference
attributes.what: A KEY REFERENCE (RFC 9635 section 7.1.1): the opaque string a client sends as `key`. It resolves to gnapSymmetricKey when that is set, and to gnapKey otherwise.

attributes.name: gnapKeyProof
attributes.what: The proofing method a key reference is bound to (section 7.1.1: "MUST be bound to a single proofing mechanism"): httpsig, jwsd or jws. Default httpsig.

attributes.name: gnapMtlsTrust
attributes.what: How a key this client proves by mutual TLS is trusted, for this client alone (#107): `pki` or `pinned`, as the realm's gnap.mtlsTrust. It can only make the realm STRICTER — `pki` where the realm is pinned — and `pinned` is refused where the realm is pki (STS-REG-0196) and ignored if the realm is made pki afterwards. Empty follows the realm. Under pki the certificate must chain to the client truststore and be issued to this entry by this realm, or carry the one RFC 8705 subject parameter it registers (oauthTlsClientAuthSubjectDn or an oauthTlsClientAuthSan* attribute).

attributes.name: gnapSymmetricKey
attributes.what: A SHARED SECRET for a key reference, base64url, at least 32 bytes — the one case GNAP allows a symmetric key, because it never crosses the wire (section 7.1.2). Sealed with the key-encryption key when keys persist, withheld from LDAP readers in product mode.

attributes.name: gnapSymmetricAlg
attributes.what: The algorithm a shared secret signs with: HS256 (default), HS384 or HS512 for jwsd and jws; hmac-sha256 for httpsig.

attributes.name: gnapClassId
attributes.from: GNAP, the console, or by hand
attributes.what: The client software's class_id (section 2.3). A registered value takes precedence over the one a request carries.

attributes.name: gnapDisplayUri
attributes.from: GNAP, the console, or by hand
attributes.what: The client's display.uri, shown on the approval page (section 2.3.2).

attributes.name: gnapLogoUri
attributes.from: GNAP, the console, or by hand
attributes.what: The client's display.logo_uri. Only a data: image is drawn; any other URI is shown as a link (section 11.16).

attributes.name: gnapFinishUri
attributes.from: GNAP (observed, development), the console, or by hand
attributes.what: An INTERACTION FINISH URI (section 2.5.2) this client may be sent back to or pushed to. A return address: in product mode a finish URI not listed here is refused.

attributes.name: gnapInteractionStartModes
attributes.what: The interaction start modes this client may use (redirect, app, user_code, user_code_uri). Empty means every mode the authorization server offers.

attributes.name: gnapAllowedAccess
attributes.what: The access types and reference strings this client may request, or this resource server may register. Empty means any.

attributes.name: gnapBearerTokens
attributes.what: FALSE refuses the bearer flag for this client with invalid_flag.

attributes.name: gnapSkipInteraction
attributes.what: TRUE makes this a TRUSTED client instance (section 2.3.3): a grant that asks for no subject information is approved with no resource owner and no interaction, and one carrying a verified user assertion is approved for that person. Honoured only for a registered entry, never one GNAP created on sight.

attributes.name: gnapAccessTokenFormat
attributes.what: The RFC 9767 token format for tokens issued to this client, or for this resource server: jwt-signed, jwt-encrypted, macaroon, biscuit or zcap.

attributes.name: gnapAccessTokenLifetimeS
attributes.what: The lifetime in seconds of access tokens issued to this client.

attributes.name: gnapResourceServerUri
attributes.what: The locations this resource server answers for. An access right whose locations start with one of these is audienced to this entry, and a token for it is minted with this resource server's format, JWE key and macaroon key.

attributes.name: gnapOwnerLookupUri
attributes.what: Where this resource server answers who owns a resource (#432 phase 5): an https URL template holding {identifier} once, in its path, e.g. https://rs.example.com/owners/{identifier}. The authorization server fetches it with the identifier percent-encoded into that segment and reads {"owner": "<DN>"} (404: nobody owns it); the person approving a right naming the identifier must be that person or a member of that group.

attributes.name: gnapJweKey
attributes.what: This resource server's PUBLIC encryption key (a JWK) for jwt-encrypted tokens, so only this resource server can read them.

attributes.name: gnapMacaroonKey
attributes.what: The macaroon ROOT KEY this resource server verifies its macaroon tokens with, base64url. Written by the authorization server when the resource server first registers a resource set; sealed with the key-encryption key when keys persist.

attributes.name: gnapScopedSignals
attributes.what: FALSE opts this web application out of Shared Signals scoping: a stream it owns then carries events about everybody, like any other receiver's.

attributes.name: spiffeWorkloadId
attributes.what: A SPIFFE ID this application is expected to hold — spiffe://<trust domain>/<path>. A SPIFFE identity gets an entry of its OWN under ou=spiffe (see spiffe/CLAUDE.md) and the registry there is what an SVID is actually issued against, so this writes nothing and reads nothing: it is the link between an application in this registry and an identity in that one, said by hand because no protocol says it.

attributes.name: appFederationRelationship
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.what:
THE FEDERATION RELATIONSHIPS THIS APPLICATION'S USERS ARE AUTHENTICATED THROUGH — each value the `fedId` of an entry under ou=federations, in THIS trust realm, whose `fedRole` is service-provider. Both halves of that are checked when it is read rather than when it is written: an identity-provider-side relationship goes the other way (this service asserts to that partner, so there is nothing to sign in to), and the register is per realm, so an id that names a relationship in another realm names nothing here.

IT HOLDS A LIST, and that is what makes an application able to offer more than one identity provider. ONE usable value with the auto-redirect on is the case this attribute was added for and it is unchanged: the browser goes straight to that partner. SEVERAL usable values draw /authn/select-idp, where the person chooses which one — home realm discovery narrowed to this application's partners rather than performed against every relationship this service has. They need not share a protocol: a SAML 2.0 partner and an OpenID Connect one are two values here and two buttons there, because what the list names is where a person can be authenticated and not how.

A value that names a relationship this service cannot use is REPORTED on the screen rather than dropped, one line per value: a list of three whose middle entry is disabled must not look like a list of two.

It is WRITTEN BY NOBODY. No protocol presents it and no sighting derives it — an application's home identity provider is an arrangement somebody made, not something this service can observe — so it is editable and it starts empty.

attributes.name: appFederationAutoRedirect
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.what:
TRUE if a person signing in to this application should be sent STRAIGHT to the partner named above, without the sign-in screen in between. This is home realm discovery done by configuration instead of by asking, which is what a deployment with one federated identity provider actually does.

It is TRUE BY DEFAULT once a relationship is named, because naming one and then having to click a button is the state nobody wants; set it FALSE to keep the screen, where the partners are then the only buttons offered. An absent value therefore means "yes" here and not "unknown", which is the opposite of what RFC 7591 section 2 makes an omitted boolean mean — said out loud because the two rules meet on one entry.

WITH SEVERAL RELATIONSHIPS NAMED IT MEANS EXACTLY WHAT IT ALWAYS MEANT — "without the sign-in screen" — and what changes is what that leaves. With one it is a redirect straight to the partner. With several it is the chooser at /authn/select-idp: one button per partner and no password field, which is the sign-in screen's job done without the sign-in screen. What it never means is "pick one for them"; there is no value of a boolean that can say which identity provider somebody's employer is.

FALSE with several named is therefore the SCREEN, with one button per partner under the password box — the same thing FALSE has always done, with the partners plural.

With no relationship named it does nothing at all, rather than being an error: the two are edited separately and a value left behind by a relationship that was cleared should not refuse the next write.

attributes.name: appAuthnPolicy
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.what:
THE AUTHENTICATION POLICY THIS APPLICATION'S PEOPLE SIGN IN UNDER: `default` (or empty), or the name of a named authentication policy of this realm (Directory > Policies). A named policy holds the first-factor mechanisms allowed (password, password-mfa, webauthn, spnego, wallet, federation; none allows every one) and the second factors allowed (password, securityKey, totp, recoveryCode, emailCode, emailLink, wallet; none leaves the realm's as it is). `default` allows every mechanism the realm's authentication policy allows.

ENFORCED at every browser sign-in to the application, in both modes: a person whose session stands on a mechanism the policy does not allow is sent to sign in again with one it does. One first-factor mechanism listed is also where the sign-in goes (`spnego` to /authn/spnego, `wallet` to /authn/wallet, `federation` to appFederationRelationship). The second factors only NARROW the realm's policy: one it has switched off stays off here.

A name no policy of this realm holds — written past the console — allows NO mechanism until the policy exists (STS-AUTHN-0536).

It is WRITTEN BY NOBODY: no protocol presents it, so it is editable and starts empty.

attributes.name: appPasskeyPolicy
attributes.from: the console, the management API, or by hand
attributes.what:
THE PASSKEY POLICY A SIGN-IN TO THIS APPLICATION IS HELD TO: `default` (or empty), or the name of a named passkey policy of this realm (Directory > Policies). It competes on precedence with the passkey policy each of the person's groups names (stsPasskeyPolicy): the lowest precedence applies, ties by name, and `default` where nothing names one.

A name no policy of this realm holds — written past the console — names nothing and is logged (STS-AUTHN-0537). A named passkey policy this attribute names cannot be deleted (STS-AUTHN-0538).

It is WRITTEN BY NOBODY: no protocol presents it, so it is editable and starts empty.

It decides the language a page is drawn in when the request, the person and the browser name none a catalog answers, and the preferredLanguage a person this application causes to be created is given. Where the person is known it competes on precedence with the locale policy each of the person's groups names (stsLocalePolicy): the lowest precedence applies, ties by name, and `default` where nothing names one.

A name no policy of this realm holds — written past the console — names nothing and is logged (STS-I18N-0013): `default` applies, as a language is all it decides. A named locale policy this attribute names cannot be deleted (STS-I18N-0014).

It is WRITTEN BY NOBODY: no protocol presents it, so it is editable and starts empty.

It competes on precedence with the password policy each of the person's groups names (stsPasswordPolicy): the lowest precedence applies, ties by name, and `default` where nothing names one. A door with no application in hand (the portal, the console, LDAP) ranks the groups' alone.

A name no policy of this realm holds — written past the console — names nothing, the group references still rank, and it is logged (STS-AUTHN-0539). A named password policy this attribute names cannot be deleted (STS-AUTHN-0540).
